segments.speaker: Mary Kinsley
segments.text: Now, it's almost a reverse. I'm speaking to people, for the most part, who want to know, "How can I make the bank foreclose on this faster?" And I talk to quite a few people who say, "Hm, perfect credit score versus $80,000 in my pocket and not upside down on this house anymore." It's really not-- it's a business decision, rather than emotional decisions.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And these are people who could continue to pay their mortgage?

segments.speaker: Mary Kinsley
segments.text: Yes. It's not illegal to breach a contract. And that's essentially what it is, it's a breach of contract. And one of the dirty little secrets of real estate is businesses do it all the time.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Strategic defaults are going to happen anytime you have plunging home values. But they were particularly bad because of something else that was going on-- another feature of the housing crisis that also shows up in our toxic asset-- speculation.

segments.speaker: Michael Braga
segments.text: This house is in your toxic asset.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This is one of ours?

segments.speaker: Michael Braga
segments.text: Yeah, this is one of yours, that's your house.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This is Michael Braga, the investigative reporter who's been helping us. This house we're looking at was bought in 2005, at the height of the bubble. But it seems like no one ever moved in, and unlike Richard's condo, it looks like no one ever intended to. Today there are dead palm trees in the front yard with the tops cut off, just eight feet of trunk sticking out of the ground. But the house has promise.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh wow, they have an ocean view?

segments.speaker: Michael Braga
segments.text: Yeah, that's Sarasota Bay. And the pool is a little green, which means that they haven't put chlorine in it. And all the blinds are down.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I can peek inside.

segments.speaker: Michael Braga
segments.text: Inside, there's some nice white couches, and a bar that looks into the kitchen, oh, and it looks like a Brady Bunch stair case that leads up to the second floor.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This house was bought not as a dream home, not even as a second home-- it was bought in 2005 by a man named Derek Taaca. Braga tells us Taaca is a local lawyer, a purple belt Jiu Jitsu martial artist, and a real estate speculator.

segments.speaker: Michael Braga
segments.text: Derek Taaca ultimately defaulted on five loans, totaling $3.6 million, including the $991,000 loan that is in your toxic asset.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Taaca did not return our phone calls. But his story is not unusual. Of the nine people we tracked down in Florida, three were investors like Taaca-- they were speculators.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And it turns out, three out of nine was typical all over the country. According to one estimate, a third of homes bought during the bubble were investments. Waitresses, cab drivers, executives all bought homes, not to live in, but to make them money.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In Florida, you can see it all over. Homes built, dry wall hung, air conditioners installed, and no one ever moved in. They were empty in 2005, and they're still empty now.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So if one third were speculators, that still leaves 2/3. 2/3 of the people in our toxic asset probably bought their homes to live in. Some are still making their payments, some are going through defaults-- not strategic defaults, they don't have a choice.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Three, Flipper: Not the Dolphin. When David and Chana went to Florida to find some of the home owners in their toxic asset, they were not expecting speculators, or an 81 year old with a new set of morals. And they certainly didn't expect to walk into a crime scene, which is what happened next. I should just say that, if you've heard a little bit about mortgage fraud in this crisis, this next story will finally explain exactly what mortgage fraud means. Here's David and Chana.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So I'm sitting at my desk, right around the time of our trip to Florida, looking through some court documents, you know, just doing some reporting for our trip. And there's this affidavit filed by an FBI agent listing a handful of mortgages that are apparently fraudulent. There's 202 Island Circle, 1628 Bay Winds Lane-- I'm sort of half paying attention. And then I see this one address-- it's George and Sylvia Bobka. Remember them?

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: Hi, you've reached Sylvia and George, we can't get to the phone right now, but leave a message and we'll get back to you. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I remember you sent me a heavily exclamation pointed text when that happened, David.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It was so surprising. I mean there are thousands and thousands of homes in the county, a handful end up listed in this affidavit, and one of them is in our Toxie? We got the court documents from Michael Braga at the Sarasota Herald Tribune .

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And it turns out, our Toxie is linked to what could be a $100 million mortgage fraud scheme they've been reporting on. Michael told us the whole thing was masterminded by one guy, a guy the folks at the Herald Tribune called the king of the flip.

segments.speaker: Michael Braga
segments.text: He just may be the biggest case of mortgage fraud in US history. And his name is Craig Adams. And he engineered more than 80 deals, which he has told the FBI about, that were in some way fraudulent. Those 80 deals, properties, were worth about $200 million.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So Chana, before when I'd heard about mortgage fraud, I always thought of some couple fudging something on their mortgage application, but this is much, much larger.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: No, in Florida, mortgage fraud appears to have been pretty widespread and organized. The reporters at the Sarasota Herald Tribune have been looking into this one circle, led by Craig Adams, the king of the flip. And it was a kind of fraud scheme based on flipping houses back and forth for higher and higher prices. So people taking out larger and larger loans from the bank, and dividing that money up amongst themselves, among the people in the circle.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: We're going to look at how this apparently worked by following one house, this is a house on Cove Terrace in Sarasota, Florida. This one is not in our toxic asset, but George and Sylvia Bobka's house is connected to the same scheme, and their house is right down the street.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So the story of what happened at Cove Terrace begins with a man who may be the very last person to have truly loved this house. The last percent to own it before it was sold into the circle of flippers.

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: Fred Bloom is my name.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Fred Bloom?

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: Fred Bloom. Isn't Dr. Bloom a perfect name for an allergist?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Are you an allergist?

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: I am.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Dr. Bloom, the allergist, raised his two daughters in this house. And it's a really nice place, it's on a quiet street, on a cul-de-sac, it's got four bedrooms, red tile roof, it's painted sort of like, you know that Florida, salmoney kind of color? And it has a pool and a boat dock.

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: We had a little boat, and my kids enjoyed water skiing, and fishing, and family activities. At the time I owned it, it was a two story family room, with windows up above, and you could sit there and watch lightning, and you could watch the sky. Just a warm, warm feeling room, with the big windows and light. So they were good years. You can hear them sort of winding up now.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That's right, because the kids grow up, huh?

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: Exactly. It was a good time in our lives.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And there, appropriately, are the cicadas-- or whatever they are-- right as we get to the drama. The drama began the moment Dr. Bloom decided to sell this house that he had loved.

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: It occurred after my wife and I got divorced, and she moved out of town, and I stayed in the house trying to sell it, because she had half equity in the house. And it didn't sell, and it didn't sell, and it didn't sell. My wife wanted to get another Realtor, and we did, and she had the house for a three month contract. And then towards the end of her contract, she became very intent on trying to lower the price so we could sell it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What'd you think about that?

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: I wasn't happy about lowering the price, but my former wife was saying, I want my money, and the Realtor was saying, let's get it sold. And I wasn't happy about that, I was not happy about lowering the price.

segments.speaker: Candy Swick
segments.text: And then we had an offer from Craig Adams.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This is the Realtor, Candy Swick.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Now, we should just point out here that this was the year 2000. Craig Adams was not known at this time as the king of the flip, or as the alleged ring leader of the largest mortgage fraud scheme in Florida history. People called him something else. They called him real estate genius.

segments.speaker: Candy Swick
segments.text: Craig's offer was very good. It was right on the mark, and when he made the offer it was a fair price. It was like, this is good, take it and run. It's been enough time. This is a very good offer.

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: And I resisted as long as I could, and then decided the fight is over, so I caved in.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Dr. Bloom sold the house for $600,000, much less than he wanted for it. And then a few weeks later, he's at the grocery store buying groceries, and he runs into his former Cove Terrace neighbors, and he asks them, "Hey, how you doing? How are the new people on the block?"

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: And they told me that my house had sold again, and he mentioned the price of $725,000. And I was really upset. I said, that's $125,000 more than I got for it, and that was only a matter of a couple of weeks.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, it was weeks?

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: It was just a matter of a couple of weeks. I was not happy.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Dr. Bloom had no idea what was going on, and he didn't for 10 years, until he gets a phone call from one of the reporters at the Sarasota Herald Tribune . So the Sarasota Herald Tribune was looking into what seemed like a lot of illegal flipping around Florida, and Craig Adams's name came up several times including, on the Cove Terrace house.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So one of the reporters, Matthew Doig, calls up Dr. Bloom, and he says, "Do you remember the details of selling that house?" Thinking Bloom probably won't remember anything, it's been 10 years. But Bloom remembered every detail of the sale, he had held onto this resentment and to this mystery for 10 years. Why did he try to sell, for over a year, try to sell his house for $700,000, and eventually have to sell it for $600,000, and then weeks later, this guy Craig Adams turns around and sells it for $725,000. Here's that reporter, Matthew Doig.

segments.speaker: Matthew Doig
segments.text: After Dr. Bloom is out of the picture, that house is completely controlled by Craig Adams, and every time it is sold, Adams is representing both the buyer and the seller. So he's completely controlling the process.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And that house sold many, many times. And in fact, to Dr. Bloom, it looked like he sold the house to Craig Adams, but Craig Adams actually got his friend Steve Wexler to sign for it. So Steve Wexler buys it from Dr. Bloom, and then Steve Wexler sells it to John Keyworth for $725,000, who sells it to Craig Adams-- who actually buys it at one point-- for $1.1 million, who sells it to Kelly West for almost one and a half million, who sells it again to Charles Scott Abel for close to $2 million.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So it sells five times in four years, and basically triples in price.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah, and Dr. Bloom the whole time is really perplexed about what is happening. He still lives in the neighborhood, and the house keeps going up in price, but it doesn't look better. It kind of looks worse.

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: Occasionally I would drive by the house and drive through the neighborhood, and at various times the yard was really in disrepair.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When it was in disrepair, did it look like no one was living here?

segments.speaker: Fred Bloom
segments.text: Yes. It looked like it was vacant.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So the way the Tribune lays this out, Keyworth, Wexler, all these guys were connected to Adams. They were part of his circle. The idea here is that with each sale, the new owner would take out a mortgage loan and use that to pay the previous owner for the house. The previous owner has now made money, because he sold it for more than he bought it for. And that profit, allegedly, gets split among the players.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So I borrow $600,000 from the bank to buy the house, and then a year later, I sell it to my buddy Keyworth for $800,000. Keyworth gets a loan from the bank, $800,000. And since we're working together, we now have just made $200,000 to split between us. That's the allegation anyway, it's still working its way through the legal system.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: When the housing bubble popped in 2007, the Cove Terrace house was owned by yet another associate of Craig Adams's, and he defaults on more than $2 million in loans. The bank forecloses on the house.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And this is when Candy Swick, Dr. Bloom's real estate agent, finally figures out something funny has been going on. She has another client interested in the Cove Terrace house, and for the second time, 10 years later, she pulls up the listing.

segments.speaker: Candy Swick
segments.text: Oh my gosh.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What did it look like?

segments.speaker: Candy Swick
segments.text: It looked like it had been sold every couple of years. And I see, Craig Adams, listed and sold. Craig Adams, listed and sold. Craig Adams, listed and sold. Craig Adams, listed and sold. And it's like, this is not right.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Not right and isn't it also stupid? This is the thing that always confused me about this kind of fraud. Because at the end of the day, all you've done is inflate the value of a house and take out larger and larger loans. And at the end, you've just got this bigger loan than you started with. You've still got to repay that. What the hell were the people in this circle thinking?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Well, in some ways, it could be the perfect crime. The last guy defaults on the house, as he did with Craig Adams's house, and that guy's credit is ruined, but he and everyone else gets to keep the money from the sales. And it's a lot of money. Though Guy Cecala, publisher of Inside Mortgage Finance , says he doesn't think these guys were that methodical.

segments.speaker: Guy Cecala
segments.text: There wasn't a great exit strategy. In hindsight, these weren't geniuses figuring out these plans, because they had a lot of pitfalls. Most of them saw quick money right away and weren't figuring out how it was going to play out over time.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Craig Adams, the king of the flip, is now an FBI informant, helping the feds investigate the circle, according to the guys at the Herald Tribune . The closing agent, who did a lot of the paper work for Craig Adams's deals on this, has been arrested. Adams did not return our calls.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [MUSIC - "THE TOXIE SONG" BY JAMES GAMMON]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So, David, I think we can say that our dream that Toxie would be an encyclopedia of the financial crisis, that part's working out.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yeah, she's got a retired guy walking away from his home, speculators, possibly fraud, and of course, some investors who bought the toxic asset without really knowing what the hell they were doing.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, why carpenters in New Jersey hate Toxie. That's in a minute, from Chicago Public Radio and Public Radio International when our program continues. It's This American Life, I'm Ira Glass. Each week on our show, of course, we choose a theme, bring you different kinds of stories on that theme. Today's show, Toxie. We try to understand the entire economic crisis through the story of a single toxic asset. The reporters on our story today are Planet Money's David Kestenbaum and Chana Joffe-Walt. We've arrived at act four of our show.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Four, Villains and How to Sue Them. January, February, these were happy months for Toxie, the toxic asset. Our team bought it in January for a thousand. In February, just like they hoped, first payment came in, a check for $141. And then, things started to take a turn. March's check was a lot less-- $44.81. Toxie was getting sick, quickly. So David and Chana called Wit Solberg in Kansas City, the guy who helped them buy Toxie in the first place.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: We have a lot of questions for you.

segments.speaker: Wit Solber
segments.text: Yeah. I imagine you do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Questions with no clear answer. Meanwhile, other things were happening. Chana got an email. Looked urgent.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Subject, do you know your toxic asset is being sued. Immediate thought, what the hell does that mean? In a moment of confusion, I thought, wait, are we being sued? In the end, it turns out the lawsuit is against the creators of our toxic asset. And the man doing the suing is as close as we could ever get to Toxie's previous owner.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: When we bought Toxie in Kansas City, we had no idea who we were buying her from. We pictured a bank, we pictured a Wall Street guy with a nice car driving down the West Side Highway. And we kept searching for him. We called out for him on national radio, on television. If you owned this bond, please get in touch with us. We didn't hear anything. We put an ad in what we imagined was his favorite publication, a newsletter called Asset Backed Alert, nothing.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But this law suit, this law suit got us someone close, a toxic asset investor who bought a close sibling of Toxie. His name is George Laufenberg. And meeting him, we realized, maybe we were looking in the wrong circles.

segments.speaker: George Laufenberg
segments.text: I'm actually a carpenter out of Local 623, Atlantic City, and I've been a member of the Carpenters Union since 1972, which puts me at about 38 years.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: George is the administrative manager of the New Jersey Carpenters Funds. He manages their pension fund, their health benefits, and their vacation fund. He bought his Toxie as an investment for the vacation fund. And that is the last you're going to hear from George, because George, in his effort to sue Toxie's creators, has hired a lawyer, who prefers to speak for him.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: George owns what you could call Toxie's younger sister. So Toxie's real name is HVMLT2005, that stands for Harbor View Mortgage Loan Trust 2005, because all the mortgages in ours were from 2005. The carpenters have HVMLT2006, so they bought the 2006 model with 2006 mortgages. Same people put her together just a year later.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Though as George's lawyer is quick to point out, George bought his Toxie way back when no one knew she was Toxie. He did not, like us, buy his as an experiment. He didn't go to Kansas City to rifle through the bargain basement. He bought what he thought was a pristine investment grade bond and paid full price. The carpenters spent $100,000, and that investment is now worth just $5,000.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So George the carpenter is furious, and he's trying to do something we've been trying to do-- figure out what's going on inside a single toxic asset.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The only difference is, we have Google and a phone, the carpenters have a team of fancy Manhattan lawyers, including Joel Laitman.

segments.speaker: Joel Laitman
segments.text: It's a complex chain of people involved.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So is it hard sometimes to figure out who to sue?

segments.speaker: Joel Laitman
segments.text: You just have to read the offering documents very carefully.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Just like 5,000 pages, right?

segments.speaker: Joel Laitman
segments.text: Yeah. Just read them and read them again.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: We're sitting in this conference room, and in front of Joel Laitman there is a huge stack of papers, almost up to my collar bone, with colored tabs, big blocked out, highlighted sections, basically reconstructing, in more detail than what we have done, who made this monster? Who is at fault? He's asking the question most of us would love to know an answer to. Who is to blame for these things? Though, as a lawyer, he's asking that with a definite goal in mind-- who can he sue?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Well, let's run through the possible suspects. Toxie's life, and the life of her sibling that the carpenters bought, started with a huge subprime mortgage lender, Countrywide. Countrywide gave out all the loans in Toxie, all those loans that are going bad. But Countrywide collapsed. They're not around anymore.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK, so how about the rating agencies? They rated this stuff as very good investments. Maybe you can sue them. The lawyers tried that. The judge dismissed it. Like most cases against rating agencies, the rating agencies argue, "We're just like movie critics or restaurant reviewers, we're expressing an opinion protected by the First Amendment."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So that leaves the sellers of the toxic asset. In this case, the Royal Bank of Scotland, RBS. They bought mortgages from Countrywide, packaged them into complex securities, and they were the guys who sold them as super safe investments to people like George the carpenter and his pension fund.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The problem with that is you can't just say, look, RBS sold me this thing that's now worthless. RBS could always argue, we didn't know it was going to be worthless. No, you have to show-- you have to prove-- they misled you in some way. And so Joel, the carpenters' lawyer, went on a quest for what is the smoking gun of securities lawyerdom-- a misstatement.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: A misstatement. Not a bunch of secret emails conspiring against the carpenters, not a clandestine recording of an RBS banker plot.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: No, a tiny technical phrase, maybe a couple, buried deep in documents that came with the toxic asset that the lawyers can prove would mislead an investor.

segments.speaker: Joel Laitman
segments.text: To find a misstatement or omission, you have to read the whole thing, many times.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Where is that, do you actually have that tagged?

segments.speaker: Joel Laitman
segments.text: Yeah, sure.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So here we're on page 81.

segments.speaker: Joel Laitman
segments.text: It starts at 80-- this is mortgage loan origination is the section, Countrywide. All of this.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And you're underlining over here.

segments.speaker: Joel Laitman
segments.text: Yeah, very exciting. It actually was exciting.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Page 81 of the offering document put out by RBS when they sold the toxic asset, Laitman found what he thinks is his misstatement. Three lines stating that the underlying collateral in the mortgage backed securities had underwriting guidelines that required a credit check-- a credit check that does not seem to have been performed on all of these loans. Ladies and gentlemen, we have a case.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: There are offices of lawyers throughout the country searching for their page 81 right now. Because it's not just carpenters in New Jersey who want their money back. PIMCO, which manages the world's largest mutual fund, does too. So do Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, those huge government sponsored mortgage lenders that ended up with toxic assets. And the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The Fed, by the way, owns another of Toxie's close siblings.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Investors all over the globe want their money back, potentially, $200 billion they believe they are owed, because somewhere, in some document, someone misrepresented what they were selling. These investors lost a lot of money, and they want someone to pay.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: If you win, who pays you?

segments.speaker: Joel Laitman
segments.text: It'll be the defendants who are in the case, so we're talking about--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: RBS?

segments.speaker: Joel Laitman
segments.text: RBS.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And that may sound satisfying, RBS sold these guys a bum investment. Who cares if it's a tiny misstatement in thousands of pages that probably no on ever read? It's like Al Capone getting caught on tax evasion. Justice is still being served, the little guy carpenters are getting justice from the big, rich, international bank.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: But there's a but.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Guess who owns RBS? The British taxpayers. RBS, like other big banks, failed. RBS failed so spectacularly that the British government ended up taking over the bank, investing billions of dollars of taxpayer money to keep RBS afloat.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Which means, if this suit is successful, it won't be fat cat RBS bankers paying back the carpenters, it'll be regular British taxpayers.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What pub is this?

segments.speaker: Chris Hayes
segments.text: The Marquis of Westminster, 50 Warwick Way, London, UK.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You're the manager?

segments.speaker: Chris Hayes
segments.text: I'm the owner.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Are you a British tax payer?

segments.speaker: Chris Hayes
segments.text: I am.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And what do you know about the bail out of British banks?

segments.speaker: Chris Hayes
segments.text: What do I know? I know that the banks lost money, and we paid-- I think the Royal Bank of Scotland-- 74% we bought them out. Bought their [UNINTELLIGIBLE].

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So in some senses, you own RBS?

segments.speaker: Chris Hayes
segments.text: We do, yeah, the tax payer does.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You and the guys in your pub?

segments.speaker: Chris Hayes
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How did you feel about it?

segments.speaker: Chris Hayes
segments.text: You know, I think it's outrageous. Because at the end of the day, these guys risk a hell of a lot, and if that risk pays off, they get paid a hell a lot of money. I think it's disgusting, personally.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did you feel like it was necessary, though?

segments.speaker: Chris Hayes
segments.text: What, that we bailed them out? No, I'd let them go under. [BLEEP], that's what I say.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Chris Hayes, the owner of the Marquis of Westminster pub. And it's actually a lot worse than Chris thought. British taxpayers now have an 84% stake in the bank. I told him about the carpenters and how they lost so much money, how they were suing RBS, which, as a British citizen, Chris the pub owner now partially owns. And when I told him that, he got a little more thoughtful.

segments.speaker: Chris Hayes
segments.text: When you buy something, I suppose you take the responsibility of what the company's done. So I suppose it's inevitable, really, to a certain degree. We're buying into their mistakes, I suppose. If it's a bunch of average men on the street trying to get their money back, I suppose I wouldn't mind so much. I mean, if American Express or BP or somebody were filing the suit, then I'd be a little bit more reticent in giving the money. But, you know, it's a bunch of carpenters. And good luck to them.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You don't mind if your money goes to them?

segments.speaker: Chris Hayes
segments.text: No, I don't mind. I mean, it's far removed from me, isn't it? If I was asked to actually physically put my hand in my pocket and hand the money over, it'd be different, wouldn't it?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That brings us to Act Five, Toxie in a Coma. I Know, It's Serious.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: After the initial scare in March, when our monthly check was only $44, Toxie looked like she was recovering. The next check we got in April was for almost double that-- $72. But then, in May, a brutal wake up call from Wit Solberg.

segments.speaker: Wit Solberg
segments.text: Well the patient, Toxie, didn't get a payment this month.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: In other words-- so we're supposed to get a check every month, how much is our check for this month?

segments.speaker: Wit Solberg
segments.text: It's for zero.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Zero?

segments.speaker: Wit Solberg
segments.text: Yeah, there wasn't a check.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Wait, wait, nothing? We're not getting anything?

segments.speaker: Wit Solberg
segments.text: Hey, you're still alive though.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: She's sort of in a coma.

segments.speaker: Wit Solberg
segments.text: A dazed state.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: A dazed state.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: We have made back half of our money, how should we feel right now?

segments.speaker: Wit Solberg
segments.text: At least you got half. Right? The glass is half full.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Seriously? The glass is half full? We got a check for zero this month.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: That's the other half of the glass.

segments.speaker: Wit Solberg
segments.text: That's the other half of the glass. No, that's right.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This wasn't the way it was supposed to happen. Back in the bond cave Rob had explained to us that we'd get checks for roughly the same amount each month, and then one day they'd stop. They're not supposed to go up and down, and they're definitely not supposed to be for $0.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So we spent $1,000. If Toxie stayed in a coma, we'd be out a lot of money. To try to sort out what was going on, we brought in Samir Noriega and Steve Marcus from NPM Capital. Samir used to trade Toxie's ancestors at JP Morgan. And he pulled up Toxie's paperwork and looked at it sort of the way a doctor looks at an x-ray, and pointed.

segments.speaker: Samir Noriega
segments.text: Here, I'll show you, real quick.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So he finds a loan in Brentwood, California, for $696,000, and he tells us, something big happened to this Brentwood guy this last month.

segments.speaker: Samir Noriega
segments.text: In this case, here you have $200,000 that were forgiven, of principal.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So you can see there, so they really just said, "Don't worry about that $200,000, you don't have to pay it."

segments.speaker: Samir Noriega
segments.text: Yeah, that was forgiven. This was deferred.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: They forgave $200,000?

segments.speaker: Samir Noriega
segments.text: That's what it looks like.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: What're they doing? I mean, I feel for that person, but that was money we were supposed to be getting some of.

segments.speaker: Steve Marcus
segments.text: In essence, because of their forgiving that homeowner that principal balance, it's affecting Toxie. So their forgiving is at your expense.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Loan modification. This was a real surprise to me, because usually you hear, number one, how loan modifications aren't happening enough, and number two, how they're good for everyone. If you modify a loan, you can keep a family in their home-- that's good for them-- and it's good for the lender, who doesn't have to foreclose on the house and sell it for what could be an even bigger loss.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: But there is one group of people it is not good for-- us. And this is where, I'm afraid, we have to dig into the toxic asset paperwork. We have to explain the line. So the way these mortgage backed securities work is that us and all the other investors who collectively own these 2,000 mortgages, we are basically standing in line to get paid. Every month, money comes in from people's mortgage checks, but that money first gets used to pay the investors standing in front of the line, then the people behind them, then the people behind them.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And we are standing way at the back of the line. And that's why our slice of this thing is toxic, that's why we got it so cheap. The people in the front paid more than us. So loan modification's bad for us. This Brentwood, California guy, he's got a smaller mortgage now, which means he's writing a smaller mortgage check each month, which means that pile of mortgages is just a little bit smaller, with less money coming in.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This month, just six mortgages in Toxie got modified, but that was enough so that the money ran out just before it got to us, at the last place in line.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This is one reason why it's been difficult to arrange loan work outs, to help people who can no longer make their payments, because there's a whole bunch of people like us who lose money when you do. I ask Samir, do investors like us call the bank and say, "Stop doing these modifications, you're killing me."

segments.speaker: Samir Noriega
segments.text: You could do that.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Would you do that if you owned this?

segments.speaker: Samir Noriega
segments.text: I own some of them, so I do that, but they don't care.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They might care, but there's a lot of pressure the other way. Some investors at the front of the line want the banks to do modifications, because any money that comes in goes to them first. The government wants banks to do modifications and has programs to encourage it, and homeowners want them, too.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So when Samir is looking at Toxie's numbers on the screen, he's pretty pessimistic. In fact, there's only one way that things are going to turn around.

segments.speaker: Samir Noriega
segments.text: If everyone won the lottery in this pool, however unlikely that is, and they all pay their mortgage entirely, you'd be getting close to $75,000.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Excellent. Then Toxie would be alive and healthy again.

segments.speaker: Samir Noriega
segments.text: It's still alive. As long as you have an outstanding principal balance, there's hope, but it's fading very quickly.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: September 19, 2010. It was pretty clear where we were headed. I went through blame, anger, denial, and then we got the call.

segments.speaker: Wit Solberg
segments.text: Well, the day has come. Toxie has officially died.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's over?

segments.speaker: Wit Solberg
segments.text: It is over.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That means there's no chance we're getting any more checks?

segments.speaker: Wit Solberg
segments.text: She's dead, Chana. She's not coming back.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: We'd bought Toxie for $1,000, and at the time of death, we had made back $449.06.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: In trying to find comfort in that moment, I console myself with this thought-- with Toxie's demise, we are one step closer to the end of this financial crisis. Now we have an answer to that big question, what are toxic assets worth? The question that's vexed governments, and big banks, and the world's finance ministers-- at least for our one toxic asset, we now know the answer-- she was worth $449.06.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Although Wit, who sees these things traded every day-- billions of dollars worth-- did not feel like this meant closure.

segments.speaker: Wit Solberg
segments.text: We're in like the third inning, if you will, on the toxic asset business. There's still a lot more that's sitting in people's balance sheets, you know, waiting for the day that they're able to sell. They're not going away anytime soon.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In other words, Toxie is survived by millions of investors and homeowners, who are part of some other toxic asset story. We still don't know how those stories are going to end. The economy's more stable than it was, but housing is still a big, big unknown thing.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I turned off the live video cam pointing at the stack of paper that was Toxie. And Chana, you scattered the remains. And by that I mean you handed out the money we got back from Toxie to our colleagues at Planet Money.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: So this is it? This is what Toxie has come down to?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh no, wait, here.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: She brings out the change.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And 80 cents, here you go.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: This is so depressing.

segments.speaker: Caitlin Kenney
segments.text: Wait, does that mean we're all only getting that much back?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: We turned your $200 into $89.

segments.speaker: Caitlin Kenney
segments.text: It's really depressing that this is all that's left of Toxie.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That's it.

segments.speaker: Jacob Goldstein
segments.text: So I've been sitting here lurking--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: That's Planet Money blogger Jacob Goldstein, who wasn't part of the staff when we bought Toxie. And he was sitting in the room, watching us each get our $89.80.

segments.speaker: Jacob Goldstein
segments.text: So look, I have a proposition, basically. It's very safe.

segments.speaker: Caitlin Kenney
segments.text: Sounds familiar.

segments.speaker: Jacob Goldstein
segments.text: And it involves you giving me $89.80, each of you. You have it there sitting in front of you. Adam, you already said it doesn't feel like a lot of money. I want you to take that money right now, put it in my hand, because I have-- what for all of history has been-- the very definition of a sound investment. Gold.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Gold?

segments.speaker: Jacob Goldstein
segments.text: One word. We're going to buy whatever, a penny size piece of gold, that will be our rock.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And you're going to bring in that gold, we're going to see the gold?

segments.speaker: Jacob Goldstein
segments.text: We are going to have what you call a gold.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: On October 4, Jacob and I went to the diamond district in New York City with Toxie's remains in a mason jar, and we bought a shiny gold coin. It cost $419, twice as much as it would have cost three years ago, which means that yes, it might be a bubble. But this time, if we lose money, at least we got in on the way up instead of the way down.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
